newsitem.title: INDIA: India sees no inflation impact from excise rises.
newsitem.headline: India sees no inflation impact from excise rises.

text.p: Higher taxes on some goods and services will not push up Indian's inflation rate in 1997/98 (April-March), and tax revenues will rise despite cuts in corporate and personal rates, Finance Ministry officials said on Saturday.
"We are very confident that you will see a softening of inflationary pressure because of this budget," Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia told a news conference on the 1997/98 budget.
Shankar Acharya, the ministry's chief economic adviser, said the prices of some goods might rise because of increases in excise rates, but there would be no upward pressure on overall prices.
On Friday, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed increasing levies on jellies, jams, sauces, soups, cigarettes and pens costing more than 100 rupees ($2.80) apiece.
He also proposed extending a service tax to road transport, consulting engineers, custom house agents, air travel agents, tour operators, outdoor caterers and manpower recruitment agencies.
"These might have some very, very minor effects on those products, but I don't think it will be at all significant," Acharya said.
"If we take the overall package, our expectation is these tax proposals will not lead to additional pressure on prices."

Earlier on Saturday, Acharya said he expected inflation as measured by the wholesale price index to average between 6.5 and 7.0 percent in 1997/98. In the week ended February 8, the annual rate was 7.99 percent.

Revenue Secretary N.K. Singh noted that the 1997/98 budget forecast a 16 percent increase in tax revenue to 1,533.47 billion rupees from 1,323.19 billion in 1996/97, despite reductions in corporate and personal income tax rates.

He said corporate tax revenue was projected to rise by about 12 percent to 218.6 billion rupees, income tax revenue by 18 percent to 217.0 billion, customs revenue by 20 percent to 525.5 billion and excise duties by 12 percent to 522.0 billion.
Singh said there were risks in cutting the corporate and income tax rates, but that they were outweighed by opportunities.
He said the reduction in the corporate rate to 35 percent from 40 percent would spur growth and lead to higher revenues.
As for personal income taxes, he said a proposed voluntary compliance scheme was expected to widen the tax base, currently limited to 12 million people in a country of 936 million.
Under the scheme, citizens living in large cities who satisfy two of four economic criteria must file income tax returns.
The criteria are ownership of a four-wheel vehicle, occupation of immovable property meeting certain, as yet unspecified guidelines, owership of a telephone and foreign travel in the previous year.
The revenue secretary said he expected the new scheme to double the number of taxpayers over the next two to three years.

Singh said he expected the compliance programme to be more effective than past measures in drawing in new taxpayers, partly because of a reduction in the top personal income tax rate to 30 percent from 40 percent.
He said the lower rate approximated the cost of managing "black money".
Also, new taxpayers would pay at the lower rate of 30 percent under the proposed scheme, and not at the higher rate that prevailed when they earned the money.
"I expect this scheme to have a much better response," Singh said.

The revenue secretary said the lowering of the personal tax rates had the benefit of bringing India's rates more closely in line with those of the rest of Asia. That, he said, would discourage capital flight.
